intro: Welcome back! Today's lesson is about pronouns — short words like I, you, he, she and they that replace names, plus my, your and her for things that belong to people. Indonesian uses 'dia' for both he and she, so English needs a little extra care here. Warm-up: what word do you use in English to talk about yourself?
teachingNotes: Indonesian 'dia' maps to he OR she (and 'it' for things) — the most common error is mixing he/she.
Possessives come BEFORE the noun in English: my book (buku saya). Learners often reverse this.
Keep sentences very short; avoid verb tenses beyond 'is/are' used in examples.

his / her follow the OWNER, not the thing owned: Budi loves his mother (the mother is a woman, but the owner Budi is a man). Indonesian -nya is the same for everyone (ibunya), so learners often choose by the thing. Point this out whenever a man owns something female or the other way round.

Explain the terms in plain Indonesian the first time: kata ganti (pronoun) = a short word used instead of a name; subjek = who or what the sentence is about, the one doing something (Rina, my mother, the phone); kata benda (noun) = a word for a person, thing or place (bag, car, mother).

is / are / am appear in the examples but are taught later (a0-to-be-basics). If asked: Indonesian needs no word there (Dia baik), English does; I → am, he/she/it → is, we/you/they → are. Don't go further.
One English word, two Indonesian ones: we = kami AND kita; you / your = one person or many (kamu, Anda, kalian). I is always a capital letter, even mid-sentence (Andi and I).
'They' for one person whose sex you don't know is a special use; say so, so it doesn't seem to break 'they = more than one'.

keyPoints.title: Subject pronouns
keyPoints.explanation: I, you, he (a man/boy), she (a woman/girl), it (a thing or animal), we, they. Use them in place of a name at the start of a sentence.

examples.en: Andi is my friend. He is tall.
Rina is a doctor. She is kind.

keyPoints.title: Possessive adjectives
keyPoints.explanation: my, your, his, her, its, our, their show who owns something. They go BEFORE the noun.

examples.en: Budi and Sari love their cat.
examples.id: Budi dan Sari menyayangi kucing mereka.

keyPoints.title: Replacing nouns
keyPoints.explanation: One person: he or she. One thing: it. Two or more people or things: they. You + me: we.

examples.en: The phone is new. It is black.
My parents are at home. They are happy.
examples.id: Orang tua saya di rumah. Mereka senang.

Complete: I have a car. This is ___ car.
Replace the words in capitals with a pronoun: THE BOOKS are on the table.

independentPractice.prompt: Andi and I are students. ___ are in class. (Which pronoun?)
Complete: Budi has a dog. ___ dog is small.
independentPractice.hint: The dog belongs to a man.

assessment.prompt: My brother is 20. ___ is a student. (Write the pronoun.)
Sari and Dewi are sisters. ___ live in Bandung.
Complete: We have a new house. ___ house is big.
Rewrite with a pronoun for the words in capitals: THE COFFEE is hot.
assessment.rubric: Correct: It is hot. Accept just 'It'.

blocks.text: A **pronoun** is a short word you use instead of a name: *Rina* → **she**. A **subject pronoun** replaces the **subject**: who or what the sentence is about, the one **doing** something, usually at the start of the sentence (*Rina, my mother, the phone*). Indonesian *dia* becomes **he** (a man or boy) or **she** (a woman or girl). Things and animals are **it**.

id.text: **Kata ganti** adalah kata pendek yang dipakai sebagai pengganti nama: *Rina* → **she**. **Kata ganti subjek** menggantikan **subjek**: siapa atau apa yang dibicarakan, yang **melakukan** sesuatu, biasanya di awal kalimat (*Rina, my mother, the phone*). *Dia* dalam bahasa Indonesia menjadi **he** (laki-laki) atau **she** (perempuan). Benda dan hewan memakai **it**.

blocks.text:
Watch out for these:
- **we** = *kami* **and** *kita*. English has one word for both.
- **you** = *kamu, Anda* **and** *kalian*: one person or many, it's the same word.
- **I** is always written with a capital letter, even in the middle of a sentence: *Andi and I*.
- After these words you'll see **am**, **is** or **are** (*She is kind. They are happy.*). Indonesian needs no word there (*Dia baik*), but English does: I → **am**, he / she / it → **is**, we / you / they → **are**. You'll learn this properly in a later lesson; for now just notice it.

id.text:
Perhatikan ini:
- **we** = *kami* **dan** *kita*. Bahasa Inggris memakai satu kata untuk keduanya.
- **you** = *kamu, Anda* **dan** *kalian*: satu orang atau banyak, katanya sama.
- **I** selalu ditulis dengan huruf kapital, bahkan di tengah kalimat: *Andi and I*.
- Setelah kata-kata ini kamu akan melihat **am**, **is** atau **are** (*She is kind. They are happy.*). Bahasa Indonesia tidak butuh kata di situ (*Dia baik*), tapi bahasa Inggris butuh: I → **am**, he / she / it → **is**, we / you / they → **are**. Ini akan kamu pelajari lebih lengkap di pelajaran berikutnya; untuk sekarang cukup diperhatikan saja.

blocks.prompt: Rina is a doctor. ___ works at a hospital.
blocks.explain: Rina is a woman, so we use she.

material.title: Possessive adjectives: my, your, his, her…

blocks.text: To show who owns something, put a possessive (**my, your, his, her, its, our, their**) **before** the noun. A **noun** is a word for a person, thing or place: *bag, car, mother*. Indonesian puts the owner after the noun (*tas saya*); English puts it first (**my bag**).

id.text: Untuk menunjukkan pemilik, letakkan kata kepemilikan (**my, your, his, her, its, our, their**) **sebelum** kata benda. **Kata benda** adalah kata untuk orang, benda atau tempat: *bag, car, mother*. Bahasa Indonesia menaruh pemilik di belakang (*tas saya*); bahasa Inggris di depan (**my bag**).

rows.en: I → my: This is my bag.
he → his: His car is red.
she → her: Her name is Dewi.
we → our: Our house is small.
they → their: Their cat is black.

blocks.text:
**his or her? Look at the owner, not the thing.** In Indonesian *-nya* is the same for everybody (*ibunya, mobilnya*), so it's easy to choose by the thing. English chooses by the **owner**:
- *Budi and **his** mother*: the mother is a woman, but the owner, Budi, is a man → **his**.
- *Sari calls **her** father every day*: the father is a man, but the owner, Sari, is a woman → **her**.
- **its** is for an owner that is a thing or an animal: *This is our cat. Its name is Mimi.*

id.text:
**his atau her? Lihat pemiliknya, bukan bendanya.** Dalam bahasa Indonesia *-nya* sama untuk siapa saja (*ibunya, mobilnya*), jadi mudah tertukar memilih berdasarkan bendanya. Bahasa Inggris memilih berdasarkan **pemiliknya**:
- *Budi and **his** mother*: ibunya perempuan, tapi pemiliknya, Budi, laki-laki → **his**.
- *Sari calls **her** father every day*: ayahnya laki-laki, tapi pemiliknya, Sari, perempuan → **her**.
- **its** dipakai kalau pemiliknya benda atau hewan: *This is our cat. Its name is Mimi.*

blocks.explain: Before a noun (mother) we need the possessive, not he. And why his, not her, when the mother is a woman? Look at the owner: Budi is a man, so his. (Him is a different form, never used before a noun.)

id.explain: Sebelum kata benda (mother) dibutuhkan kata kepemilikan, bukan he. Lalu kenapa his, bukan her, padahal ibunya perempuan? Lihat pemiliknya: Budi laki-laki, jadi his. (Him adalah bentuk lain yang tidak pernah dipakai sebelum kata benda.)

id.title: Kata ganti kepemilikan: my, your, his, her…

blocks.text: Don't repeat the same noun in every sentence. After you name it once, switch to a pronoun: one man → **he**, one woman → **she**, one thing → **it**, more than one → **they**, you and me → **we**.

id.text: Jangan mengulang kata benda yang sama di setiap kalimat. Setelah disebut sekali, ganti dengan kata ganti: satu laki-laki → **he**, satu perempuan → **she**, satu benda → **it**, lebih dari satu → **they**, kamu dan saya → **we**.

rows.en: The laptop is new. It is fast.
My parents are at home. They are happy.
rows.id: Orang tua saya di rumah. Mereka senang.

rows.en: Andi and I are friends. We play futsal.
rows.id: Andi dan saya berteman. Kami main futsal.

blocks.prompt: The shoes are too small. ___ are size 38.
blocks.explain: Shoes = more than one thing, so they.

id.explain: Shoes = lebih dari satu benda, jadi they.

blocks.text: At work you often talk about colleagues who aren't there: *She is in a meeting. He works in marketing.* If you don't know if someone is a man or a woman (for example in an email), English speakers often use **they** for one person. This is a special use: here *they* means that one person, not a group.

id.text: Di kantor kamu sering membicarakan rekan yang tidak ada di tempat: *She is in a meeting. He works in marketing.* Kalau tidak tahu apakah seseorang laki-laki atau perempuan (misalnya di email), penutur bahasa Inggris sering memakai **they** untuk satu orang. Ini pemakaian khusus: di sini *they* berarti satu orang itu, bukan sekelompok orang.

blocks.text: Mixing up he and she is the most common mistake for Indonesian speakers. Before you speak, picture the person.

id.text: Tertukar he dan she adalah kesalahan paling umum penutur bahasa Indonesia. Sebelum bicara, bayangkan orangnya.

suggestedQuestions: When do I use he and when she?
What's the difference between he and his?
Why does English use 'it' for things?
How do I say 'dia' if I don't know if it's a man or a woman?

id.intro: Selamat datang kembali! Pelajaran hari ini tentang kata ganti — kata pendek seperti I, you, he, she dan they untuk menggantikan nama, plus my, your dan her untuk benda milik seseorang. Bahasa Indonesia memakai 'dia' untuk laki-laki maupun perempuan, jadi bahasa Inggris perlu sedikit lebih teliti. Pemanasan: kata apa yang kamu pakai dalam bahasa Inggris untuk menyebut dirimu sendiri?
suggestedQuestions: Kapan pakai he dan kapan she?
Kenapa bahasa Inggris memakai 'it' untuk benda?
Bagaimana bilang 'dia' kalau tidak tahu laki-laki atau perempuan?
